nota: Título y descripción de cada materia en la lengua estudiada; oficial = rótulo del Core Inventory (solo inglés).

en.g.to-be.oficial: To be, including question+negatives; Past simple (to be)
en.g.to-be.descripcion_l: The verb be in the present and past: affirmative, negative and question forms.
en.g.to-be.descripcion_larga_l: The verb to be means both «ser» and «estar» in Spanish. In the present it has three forms: I am, he/she/it is, you/we/they are. In the past it has two: was and were. To make questions, put the verb before the subject (Are you ready?), and to make negatives, add not (She isn't here). We also use to be for age, hunger and feelings: I am 30, I am hungry.

en.g.present-simple.descripcion_l: Talking about routines and facts; the third-person -s ending and do/does in questions and negatives.
en.g.present-simple.descripcion_larga_l: We use the present simple for habits and routines (I work from nine to five), likes and opinions (She likes jazz) and general facts (Water boils at 100 degrees). With he, she and it the verb adds -s. Questions and negatives use do or does, and after does the verb goes back to the base form: Does he work? He doesn't work.

en.g.present-continuous.descripcion_l: Describing actions happening now and temporary situations.
en.g.present-continuous.descripcion_larga_l: The present continuous (am/is/are + verb + -ing) describes actions happening now, at the moment of speaking, or temporary situations around now (this week, these days). We don't use it for habits: for routines we use the present simple. Some verbs, like know, like or want, are not normally used in the continuous form. Remember the spelling rules: making, running, lying.

en.g.have-got.descripcion_l: Have and have got for possession, including questions and negatives.
en.g.have-got.descripcion_larga_l: Have and have got both mean that something belongs to you or is part of you: I have a car, I've got a car. With have we make questions and negatives with do or does (Do you have a pen?). With have got, have itself moves (Have you got a pen?). Do not mix the two, and remember that age uses be: I'm 25.

en.g.can.descripcion_l: Using can and can't for ability, permission and requests.
en.g.can.descripcion_larga_l: Can is a modal verb. We use it to talk about ability (I can swim), to ask for permission (Can I sit here?) and to make requests (Can you help me?). It has the same form for all persons: she can, not she cans. The next verb has no to: I can come. Questions and negatives do not use do: Can you drive? I can't drive.

en.g.there-is.descripcion_l: Saying that something exists, with some and any.
en.g.there-is.descripcion_larga_l: We use there is and there are to say that something exists or is in a place. Use there is with singular and uncountable nouns (there is a bank, there is some milk) and there are with plural nouns (there are two banks). In the past, say there was and there were. Use some in positive sentences and any in negatives and questions. Never translate «hay» with have.

en.g.articulos.titulo_l: Articles: a/an, the and zero article
en.g.articulos.oficial: Articles – Definite, indefinite; Zero article with uncountable nouns
en.g.articulos.descripcion_l: Basic use of a/an and the: first mention, unique things and the basics of no article.
en.g.articulos.descripcion_larga_l: English has two kinds of article: a/an (one, any) and the (a specific thing). Use a before a consonant sound (a university) and an before a vowel sound (an hour). Use the for things we already know or unique things, like the sun. When we talk about things in general, we use no article: I like coffee, cats are independent. Jobs always take a or an: She is a doctor.

en.g.plurales.descripcion_l: Forming regular and irregular noun plurals.
en.g.plurales.descripcion_larga_l: Most English nouns make the plural with -s: one car, two cars. Some nouns change their spelling: box becomes boxes, city becomes cities and knife becomes knives. A small group of very common nouns is irregular: man and men, child and children, foot and feet. Adjectives never take -s, so we say two big houses.

en.g.posesivos.descripcion_l: Possessive adjectives (my, your…), possessive 's and the structure with of.
en.g.posesivos.descripcion_larga_l: Possessives show who something belongs to. Possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) go before a noun: my bag, her father. His and her depend on the owner: Juan and his mother, Marta and her father. For people we usually add 's to the owner: my brother's car. For things we often use of: the end of the film.

en.g.demostrativos.descripcion_l: The demonstratives this, that, these and those.
en.g.demostrativos.descripcion_larga_l: We use this, that, these and those to show which person or thing we mean. This and these are for things near us; that and those are for things far from us. This and that are singular; these and those are plural. We also use them for time (this week, that day), on the phone (This is Marta) and to introduce people.

en.g.pronombres.descripcion_l: Subject and object personal pronouns: I/me, he/him and so on.
en.g.pronombres.descripcion_larga_l: Subject pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they) go before the verb and do the action. Object pronouns (me, you, him, her, it, us, them) go after the verb or after a preposition: She loves me, Come with us. In English the subject is always necessary, so we say It's raining and It's late, never just Is late.

en.g.imperativo.descripcion_l: Affirmative and negative imperatives for instructions and advice, plus let's for suggestions.
en.g.imperativo.descripcion_larga_l: The imperative is the base form of the verb without a subject: Sit down, Close the door, Add some salt. We use it for orders, instructions and advice. The negative is don't + verb: Don't run! With adjectives we need be: Be careful, Don't be late. To make a suggestion that includes you, use let's + verb: Let's go to the beach.

en.g.preposiciones-tiempo-lugar.titulo_l: Prepositions of place / Prepositions of time: on/in/at
en.g.preposiciones-tiempo-lugar.oficial: Prepositions of place; Prepositions of time: on/in/at
en.g.preposiciones-tiempo-lugar.descripcion_l: Using in, on and at for time and place.
en.g.preposiciones-tiempo-lugar.descripcion_larga_l: In, on and at are the most common prepositions of time and place. Use at for exact times and points (at 8 o'clock, at the bus stop), on for days, dates and surfaces (on Monday, on the table), and in for months, years, seasons and closed spaces (in July, in the kitchen, in Spain). Do not use a preposition before next, last, this or every: next week.

en.g.preguntas-wh.descripcion_l: Questions with what, where, when, who, why and how, including how much, how many and how often.
en.g.preguntas-wh.descripcion_larga_l: Wh- questions begin with a question word: what, where, when, who, why, which or how. After the question word comes an auxiliary (do, does, is, can) and then the subject: Where do you live? What time does the train leave? With the verb to be, we put be before the subject: Where are you from? How can also combine with other words: how much, how many, how old, how often.

en.g.contables.titulo_l: Countable and uncountable / Determiners: some, any, a lot of
en.g.contables.oficial: Countable and uncountable; Basic (e.g. any, some, a lot of)
en.g.contables.descripcion_l: Countable and uncountable nouns with some, any and a lot of.
en.g.contables.descripcion_larga_l: Countable nouns can be counted and have a plural form (an apple, two apples). Uncountable nouns have no plural and don't take a or an (water, money, information). This affects the article, the verb and words like some and any. Some nouns are uncountable in English but countable in Spanish: advice, information, news, furniture and homework.

en.g.past-simple.descripcion_l: Regular and irregular past forms, with did in questions and negatives.
en.g.past-simple.descripcion_larga_l: The past simple is the basic tense for finished actions at a definite time in the past: yesterday, last year, in 2010, two days ago. Regular verbs add -ed and irregular verbs have their own forms (go → went). In negatives and questions we use did / didn't + infinitive, because did already shows the past.

en.g.past-continuous.descripcion_l: Background actions in the past, often combined with when and while.
en.g.past-continuous.descripcion_larga_l: The past continuous (was / were + -ing) describes an action in progress at a moment in the past. We often use it for the background of a story, while the past simple tells the short actions that happened: I was cooking when the phone rang. Remember: when usually goes with the short action and while with the long one.

en.g.going-to.descripcion_l: Be going to for plans and for predictions based on present evidence.
en.g.going-to.descripcion_larga_l: Be going to + infinitive is a common way to talk about the future. We use it for plans and intentions we have already decided (I'm going to start a diet on Monday) and for predictions based on what we can see now (Look at the sky! It's going to rain). Remember that be is always necessary: I am going to, she is going to.

en.g.will.descripcion_l: Will for predictions, offers and decisions made at the moment of speaking.
en.g.will.descripcion_larga_l: We use will + infinitive to make predictions (I think it will rain), to decide something at the moment of speaking (I'll answer the phone), to offer help (I'll carry that), to promise (I won't tell anyone) and to ask for things (Will you help me?). The form is the same for all persons. For plans you made before, use going to.

en.g.present-perfect.descripcion_l: The present perfect for experiences, with just, already, yet, ever and never.
en.g.present-perfect.descripcion_larga_l: The present perfect (have/has + past participle) connects the past and the present. We use it for life experiences without a date (I've been to Japan), recent actions with a result now (I've lost my keys) and situations that started in the past and continue (We've lived here for ten years). If we say when something happened (yesterday, last year, ago), we use the past simple.

en.g.comparativos.descripcion_l: Comparative and superlative adjectives: -er/-est, more/most, as… as and irregular forms.
en.g.comparativos.descripcion_larga_l: We use comparatives to compare two things (cheaper than, more expensive than) and superlatives to say that one thing is first in a group (the cheapest, the most expensive). Short adjectives add -er and -est; long adjectives use more and most. Some are irregular: good, better, the best. Remember to use than, not that, after a comparative.

en.g.adverbios-frecuencia.titulo_l: Adverbs of frequency / Simple adverbs of place, manner and time
en.g.adverbios-frecuencia.oficial: Adverbs of frequency; Simple adverbs of place, manner and time
en.g.adverbios-frecuencia.descripcion_l: Frequency adverbs such as always and usually, -ly adverbs of manner, and where adverbs go in the sentence.
en.g.adverbios-frecuencia.descripcion_larga_l: Adverbs of frequency (always, usually, often, sometimes, never) tell us how often something happens. They usually go before the main verb but after the verb be: I always walk to work, but she is always late. Adverbs of manner (slowly, carefully, well) tell us how we do something and normally go after the verb and its object: She speaks English fluently.

en.g.cuantificadores.oficial: Countables and Uncountables: much/many; Wider range (e.g. all, none, not (any), enough, (a) few)
en.g.cuantificadores.descripcion_l: The quantifiers much, many, a few and a little.
en.g.cuantificadores.descripcion_larga_l: Quantifiers like much, many, a few and a little tell us how much or how many of something there is. The right word depends on the noun: we use many and a few with countable nouns (books, people) and much and a little with uncountable nouns (water, money, advice). Few and little without a mean «not enough».

en.g.obligacion.descripcion_l: Must and have to for obligation and necessity, and should for advice.
en.g.obligacion.descripcion_larga_l: We use must and have to to talk about obligation, and should to give advice. Be careful with the negative forms: mustn't means that something is not allowed, but don't have to means that something is not necessary. Must and should never take -s or to, while have to works like a normal verb: she has to, do you have to?, we had to.

en.g.verbo-ing-to.descripcion_l: Which common verbs (like, enjoy, want, decide…) are followed by -ing and which by to-infinitive.
en.g.verbo-ing-to.descripcion_larga_l: When one verb follows another, the second verb can take -ing (I enjoy reading) or to + infinitive (I want to read). It depends on the first verb, so learn them together: enjoy, finish, mind, avoid take -ing; want, decide, hope, need take to. After a preposition, always use -ing: good at drawing. Would like always takes to: I'd like to go.

en.g.posesivos-pron.descripcion_l: Possessive pronouns such as mine and yours, and the question word whose.
en.g.posesivos-pron.descripcion_larga_l: Possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs) replace a possessive adjective and a noun: my book becomes mine. They stand alone, without a noun after them and without the before them: This seat is mine. To ask who something belongs to, we use whose: Whose coat is this? Be careful: who's means who is.

en.g.primer-condicional.descripcion_l: If + present simple with will to talk about likely future situations.
en.g.primer-condicional.descripcion_larga_l: We use the first conditional to talk about a possible situation in the future and its result: If you study, you'll pass. The if-clause uses the present simple, never will. The result uses will, an imperative or a modal like can or might. Unless means if not. After when, as soon as, before and after with a future meaning, we also use the present: I'll call you when I get home.

en.g.preguntas-sujeto.descripcion_l: The difference between questions about the subject (Who called?) and about the object (Who did you call?).
en.g.preguntas-sujeto.descripcion_larga_l: When who, what or which asks about the subject, the person or thing that does the action, we do not use do, does or did: Who called you? What happened? When it asks about the object, we use the auxiliary as in other questions: Who did you call? In subject questions the verb is usually singular, even if the answer is plural: Who wants coffee?

en.g.pp-continuous.descripcion_l: Talking about the duration of an activity up to now, with for and since.
en.g.pp-continuous.descripcion_larga_l: We use the present perfect continuous (have or has been + -ing) for an activity that started in the past and is still happening now, or has just stopped. It focuses on how long: I have been waiting for an hour. Use for with a period of time and since with a starting point. Verbs like know or like use the simple form: I've known her for years.

en.g.pp-vs-past.descripcion_l: Choosing between present perfect and past simple: unfinished versus finished time.
en.g.pp-vs-past.descripcion_larga_l: Use the past simple when the time is finished and is mentioned or clear: I watched a film last night. Use the present perfect when the period continues until now or the time is not important: Have you ever been to Rome? Words like yesterday, ago and in 2019 go with the past simple; ever, never, yet, just and since usually go with the present perfect.

en.g.past-perfect.descripcion_l: Referring to an earlier point in the past.
en.g.past-perfect.descripcion_larga_l: The past perfect (had + past participle) shows that something happened before another moment in the past: When I got to the station, the train had left. It helps you tell stories clearly and explain reasons. Use it only when you go back in time; if you tell events in the order they happened, the past simple is enough.

en.g.used-to.titulo_l: Used to / Would expressing habit in the past
en.g.used-to.oficial: Used to; Would expressing habit in the past
en.g.used-to.descripcion_l: Used to and would for past habits, and used to for past states.
en.g.used-to.descripcion_larga_l: We use used to + infinitive for habits and states in the past that are not true now: I used to play football; there used to be a cinema here. Would can also describe repeated actions in stories, but not states. In questions and negatives, write use to after did. Do not confuse it with be used to + -ing, which means being accustomed to something.

en.g.futuros.titulo_l: Future Time (will & going to) / Present continuous for future
en.g.futuros.oficial: Future Time (will & going to); Present continuous for future
en.g.futuros.descripcion_l: Comparing future forms: will, going to, present continuous and present simple.
en.g.futuros.descripcion_larga_l: English has several ways to talk about the future. We use will for quick decisions, offers, promises and opinions; be going to for plans and for predictions based on what we can see; the present continuous for arrangements with a time and place; and the present simple for timetables. After when, if or as soon as we use the present, not will.

en.g.condicional-0-2.descripcion_l: The zero conditional for general truths and the second conditional for unreal present situations.
en.g.condicional-0-2.descripcion_larga_l: The zero conditional talks about things that are always true when something happens (If you heat ice, it melts). The second conditional talks about imaginary or unlikely situations now or in the future (If I had more time, I would learn Chinese). Remember: never use would after if, and use If I were you to give advice.

en.g.pasiva-basica.descripcion_l: The present and past passive: be + past participle, with by for the agent.
en.g.pasiva-basica.descripcion_larga_l: The passive voice in the present and past (is made, was built) puts the focus on the action or on the thing affected, not on the person who does it. We use it a lot in news, instructions and descriptions of processes. Form it with be in the right tense plus the past participle, and add by only when the agent is important.

en.g.relativas.descripcion_l: Defining relative clauses with who, which, that, where and whose.
en.g.relativas.descripcion_larga_l: Defining relative clauses tell us which person or thing we are talking about: The man who called you is here. We use who for people, which for things, where for places and whose for possession; that can replace who or which. If the relative pronoun is the object, we can leave it out: the film we saw. We never repeat the object: the car that I bought, not the car that I bought it.

en.g.estilo-indirecto.descripcion_l: Reporting statements: tense backshift and the difference between say and tell.
en.g.estilo-indirecto.descripcion_larga_l: Reported speech is how we tell other people what someone said, without using their exact words: She said she was tired. We usually use said or told, and the verb often moves one step into the past: am becomes was, will becomes would. Words like I, you, today and tomorrow can also change. Remember: tell needs a person after it, say does not.

en.g.deduccion-presente.titulo_l: Modals - must/can’t deduction / Modals – might, may
en.g.deduccion-presente.oficial: Modals - must/can’t deduction; Modals – might, may, will, probably
en.g.deduccion-presente.descripcion_l: Using must, might, could and can't to make deductions about the present.
en.g.deduccion-presente.descripcion_larga_l: We use modal verbs to make guesses about the present when we see some evidence. Must means we are almost sure something is true; might, may and could mean it is possible; can't means we are almost sure it is not true. Remember that mustn't is not a guess: it means something is not allowed. After the modal, use the verb without to.

en.g.reflexivos.descripcion_l: Reflexive pronouns such as myself and themselves, and the reciprocal each other.
en.g.reflexivos.descripcion_larga_l: Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves) are used when the subject and the object are the same person: She cut herself. We also use them for emphasis: I did it myself. By myself means alone. Many verbs that are reflexive in Spanish are not reflexive in English: get up, relax, get dressed, meet. For mutual actions we use each other.

en.g.so-such.oficial: Broader range of intensifiers such as too, enough
en.g.so-such.descripcion_l: Expressing degree and result with so, such, too and enough.
en.g.so-such.descripcion_larga_l: So and such make adjectives and nouns stronger: so cold, such a cold day. Too means more than you want or need, and it usually has a negative meaning: too expensive to buy. Enough means the right amount; it goes after an adjective (old enough) but before a noun (enough chairs). Each word has its own position in the sentence, so learn the patterns carefully.

en.g.question-tags.descripcion_l: Question tags (isn't it?) and polite indirect questions (Could you tell me where…?).
en.g.question-tags.descripcion_larga_l: Question tags are short questions at the end of a sentence, like isn't it? or did they?. We use the auxiliary verb of the sentence and a pronoun: a positive sentence takes a negative tag and a negative sentence takes a positive tag. Indirect questions (Could you tell me…, Do you know…) are more polite, and they use normal word order without do, does or did: Do you know where she lives?

en.g.phrasal-1.descripcion_l: Common phrasal verbs and their meanings.
en.g.phrasal-1.descripcion_larga_l: Phrasal verbs are a verb plus a particle (up, off, out, on…) with a special meaning: give up means stop doing something, find out means discover. They are very common in everyday English. Learn each one as a new word, and check if it is separable: with a pronoun, separable verbs always put it in the middle (turn it off).

en.g.futuro-continuo-perfecto.descripcion_l: Will be doing for actions in progress in the future, and will have done for completed actions.
en.g.futuro-continuo-perfecto.descripcion_larga_l: The future continuous (will be + -ing) describes an action in progress at a point in the future: This time tomorrow I'll be flying. The future perfect (will have + past participle) describes an action completed before a future point: By Friday we'll have finished. They are very useful for deadlines, plans and polite questions about other people's plans.

en.g.tercer-condicional.descripcion_l: The third conditional for the unreal past, and mixed conditionals linking a past cause to a present result.
en.g.tercer-condicional.descripcion_larga_l: The third conditional imagines a different past and its past result: If I had left earlier, I would have caught the train. Mixed conditionals combine times: a past condition with a present result (If I had taken the job, I would live in London now), or a present situation with a past result. Never use would in the if-clause, and look at time words like now or last year to choose the right form.

en.g.pasiva-completa.descripcion_l: Continuous, perfect and modal passives, and the passive with get.
en.g.pasiva-completa.descripcion_larga_l: This card covers the passive in every tense and with modal verbs: is being built, has been published, will have been finished, should have been sent. It also shows passive infinitives and gerunds (to be told, being interrupted) and the informal get passive (got stolen). The trick is simple: put be in the tense you need and add the past participle.

en.g.causativo.descripcion_l: Have something done and get someone to do something.
en.g.causativo.descripcion_larga_l: We use have or get + object + past participle when someone else does something for us, usually because we pay or ask them: I had my hair cut, we got the car repaired. It can also describe something bad that happened to us: She had her bag stolen. With a person we say have someone do something (no to) or get someone to do something (with to).

en.g.relativas-explicativas.descripcion_l: Non-defining relative clauses: commas, which referring to a whole clause, and prepositions with whom and which.
en.g.relativas-explicativas.descripcion_larga_l: Non-defining relative clauses give extra information about a person or thing we have already identified. They go between commas and you can remove them without changing the main meaning. In these clauses you cannot use that and you cannot leave out the pronoun. Which can also refer to a whole sentence: He was late, which annoyed everyone. In formal English, a preposition can go before whom or which.

en.g.estilo-indirecto-2.titulo_l: Reported questions, commands and reporting verbs
en.g.estilo-indirecto-2.descripcion_l: Reporting questions and commands, and reporting verbs such as ask, advise, deny, claim and suggest.
en.g.estilo-indirecto-2.descripcion_larga_l: This sheet goes beyond say and tell. In reported questions we use normal word order and no do: She asked where I lived. For orders and requests we use tell or ask + person + to + infinitive. Reporting verbs such as advise, deny, refuse, suggest or accuse each have their own pattern, so it is useful to learn each verb together with its structure.

en.g.deduccion-pasado.oficial: Modals of deduction and speculation; Modals – can’t have, needn’t have
en.g.deduccion-pasado.descripcion_l: Making deductions about the past with must have, might have and can't have done.
en.g.deduccion-pasado.descripcion_larga_l: Past modals of deduction let you make logical guesses about the past from the evidence you have. Use must have + past participle when you are almost sure something happened, might, may or could have when it is possible, and can't or couldn't have when you are almost sure it did not happen. The opposite of must have is can't have, not mustn't have.

en.g.wish.descripcion_l: Expressing regrets and preferences with wish, if only, would rather and it's time.
en.g.wish.descripcion_larga_l: We use wish and if only to talk about things we want to be different: wish + past simple for the present (I wish I had more time) and wish + past perfect for the past (I wish I hadn't said that). Wish + would is a complaint about someone. Would rather and it's time + subject also take the past: I'd rather you didn't smoke; it's time we left.

en.g.participiales.descripcion_l: Clauses beginning with a participle, such as Having finished… or Built in 1900…
en.g.participiales.descripcion_larga_l: Participle clauses are short clauses without a subject that replace a longer time, reason or relative clause: Feeling tired, I went to bed early; Built in 1900, the station is now a museum. They are common in formal and written English. Use -ing for active meaning, the past participle for passive meaning, and having + participle for an earlier action. The subject must be the same as in the main clause.

en.g.contraste.titulo_l: Linkers: although, in spite of, despite
en.g.contraste.oficial: Linkers: although, in spite of, despite; Connecting words expressing cause and effect, contrast etc
en.g.contraste.descripcion_l: Expressing contrast and concession with although, despite, in spite of, whereas and however.
en.g.contraste.descripcion_larga_l: Contrast linkers show that something happens in spite of a problem, or that two facts are different. What follows each linker is important: although and even though take a clause; despite and in spite of take a noun or an -ing form; however and nevertheless start a new sentence; whereas and while compare two facts. Never say despite of.

en.g.articulos-2.descripcion_l: Articles for generic reference, with institutions and with abstract nouns.
en.g.articulos-2.descripcion_larga_l: In English, general statements with plural or uncountable nouns take no article: Inflation is rising, Cats are independent. We use the when the noun is made specific (the inflation of the 1970s). Some places change meaning: in prison means serving a sentence, but at the prison means the building. We also say the poor, the elderly, play the violin, and the Alps, but Mont Blanc and France.

en.g.cuantificadores-2.titulo_l: Determiners: broad range (e.g. all the, most, both)
en.g.cuantificadores-2.oficial: Broad range (e.g. all the, most, both)
en.g.cuantificadores-2.descripcion_l: Each, every, either, neither, both and none of.
en.g.cuantificadores-2.descripcion_larga_l: Advanced quantifiers help you talk precisely about groups. Both, either and neither refer to two people or things; all and none refer to three or more. Every and each go with a singular noun, but each looks at members one by one. Remember: every never takes of, and neither is already negative, so you don't need another not.

en.g.verbo-ing-to-2.oficial: Gerund and infinitive; Verb + to + infinitive
en.g.verbo-ing-to-2.descripcion_l: Verbs whose meaning changes with -ing or to (remember, stop, try), and verb + object + infinitive.
en.g.verbo-ing-to-2.descripcion_larga_l: Some verbs can take both -ing and to + infinitive, but the meaning changes: remember doing (a memory) and remember to do (a task); stop doing (give up) and stop to do (pause for a reason). Verbs like want, ask, tell and expect take a person + to: I want you to stay, never want that. Make and let take a person + infinitive without to.

en.g.pasiva-impersonal.descripcion_l: Impersonal passive structures: It is said that… and He is said to…
en.g.pasiva-impersonal.descripcion_larga_l: Impersonal passives (It is said that…, He is said to…) are how formal English reports opinions, rumours and forecasts without saying who holds them. They are very common in news and reports: The economy is expected to grow by 2%. Choose the infinitive carefully: to do for the same time, to be doing for actions in progress, and to have done for earlier actions.

en.g.phrasal-2.titulo_l: Phrasal verbs, extended / Phrasal verbs, especially splitting
en.g.phrasal-2.oficial: Phrasal verbs, extended; Phrasal verbs, especially splitting
en.g.phrasal-2.descripcion_l: Separable and inseparable phrasal verbs, and three-part phrasal verbs.
en.g.phrasal-2.descripcion_larga_l: This card explains where the object goes with phrasal verbs. With separable verbs a pronoun always goes in the middle (turn it off). With inseparable and three-part verbs the object always goes at the end (look after him, put up with it). Remember that look forward to is followed by -ing, because to is a preposition here.

en.g.enfatico.descripcion_l: Adding emphasis with do and stressed auxiliaries, as in I do agree or She did call.
en.g.enfatico.descripcion_larga_l: Emphatic do means putting do, does or did before a verb to make a statement stronger: I do like it! You use it to disagree with someone, to insist, to accept a point before saying but, or to show strong feeling. After do, does or did, the main verb is always in the base form. With other auxiliaries, you simply stress the auxiliary when you speak.

en.g.inversion.descripcion_l: Inversion after negative or restrictive expressions: Never have I…, Not only…, Hardly… when, Little did they know.
en.g.inversion.descripcion_larga_l: When a sentence begins with a negative or restrictive expression such as never, rarely, not only, hardly or under no circumstances, English puts the auxiliary verb before the subject, as in a question: Never have I seen such a mess. If there is no auxiliary, we add do, does or did. This structure is formal and emphatic, and it is very useful in speeches and essays.

en.g.condicional-sin-if.descripcion_l: Inverted conditionals (Had I known…, Should you need…, Were it not for…) and alternatives such as provided that and unless.
en.g.condicional-sin-if.descripcion_larga_l: In formal English, we can leave out if and invert the subject with should, were or had: Should you need help, call me; Had we known, we would have come. Other words can replace if with a slightly different meaning: unless, provided that, as long as, on condition that, otherwise and but for. These structures are common in formal letters, contracts and reports.

en.g.cleft.descripcion_l: Cleft sentences for focus: It was… that… and What I need is…
en.g.cleft.descripcion_larga_l: Cleft sentences split one idea into two parts to focus on one element. With an it-cleft we highlight a person, thing, place or time: It was Maria who found the keys, It was in Rome that I met her. With a wh-cleft we put the focus at the end: What I need is a holiday, What she did was call the police. They are useful for contrast and emphasis.

en.g.subjuntivo.descripcion_l: The subjunctive after expressions like It is essential that he be…, and in formal suggestions.
en.g.subjuntivo.descripcion_larga_l: The English subjunctive uses the base form of the verb for every person: It is essential that he be on time; They demanded that she leave. It appears after verbs, adjectives and nouns of demand, recommendation or importance, mostly in formal English. The negative is not + base form, without do. Were is used for all persons in unreal conditions and after wish or if only.

en.g.modales-pasado.oficial: Modals in the past; Modals – should have/might have/etc
en.g.modales-pasado.descripcion_l: Nuances of past modals: needn't have versus didn't need to, should have and would have.
en.g.modales-pasado.descripcion_larga_l: Past modals (modal + have + past participle) let us talk about the past with nuance: we make deductions (it must have rained), rule things out (she can't have finished), suggest possibilities (he might have missed the bus), criticise or regret (you should have told me) and imagine results (I would have helped). Pay attention to the difference between needn't have done and didn't need to do.

en.g.futuro-pasado.descripcion_l: Talking about the future from a past viewpoint: was going to, was to, was about to and would.
en.g.futuro-pasado.descripcion_larga_l: When we tell a story about the past, we often need to talk about things that were still in the future at that time. English puts its future forms into the past: was going to for intentions, would for reported promises, was to for official plans or destiny, and was about to for something that was going to happen very soon. Each form keeps its own meaning.

en.g.elipsis.descripcion_l: Avoiding repetition with so, not, do so and one/ones.
en.g.elipsis.descripcion_larga_l: Ellipsis and substitution help you avoid repeating words. English leaves something out or uses a short word instead: so, not, one, do so, an auxiliary on its own, or to without a verb. Using them well makes your speech sound natural and fluent. Spanish speakers often find this hard, because Spanish can simply drop words, while English usually keeps a small word to support the sentence.

en.g.nominalizacion.descripcion_l: Turning verbs and adjectives into nouns for a formal written style, e.g. the introduction of…, the rise in…
en.g.nominalizacion.descripcion_larga_l: Nominalisation means turning verbs and adjectives into nouns: introduce becomes the introduction of, and available becomes the availability of. It makes texts more formal, compact and impersonal, so it is typical of reports, economic journalism and academic presentations. The key difficulties are choosing the correct noun ending and the correct preposition, for example a rise in prices or the decision to act.

en.g.fronting.descripcion_l: Moving information to the start of the sentence for emphasis or cohesion.
en.g.fronting.descripcion_larga_l: Fronting means moving part of a sentence to the beginning to give it emphasis or to link it with the previous idea, as in So strong was the wind that trees fell. Because English word order is usually fixed, fronting is very noticeable. Sometimes it requires inversion of the subject and the verb, and sometimes it does not, so you need to learn the patterns.

en.g.participiales-2.descripcion_l: Perfect, passive and being participle clauses, such as Having been told… or Being the eldest…
en.g.participiales-2.descripcion_larga_l: Advanced participle clauses (Having been told…, Being the eldest…, Weather permitting…) let you say a reason, a time or a condition in very few words. They are common in formal writing, news and reports. The key rule is that the hidden subject of the participle must be the same as the subject of the main clause; if not, you must state it or rewrite the sentence.

en.g.formulas-subjuntivo.descripcion_l: Fixed expressions that keep the subjunctive, such as be that as it may, come what may and so be it.
en.g.formulas-subjuntivo.descripcion_larga_l: Some fixed English expressions keep the old subjunctive: the verb is in its base form (be, come, suffice) and often comes before the subject, as in be that as it may or come what may. You cannot build new ones; you learn them as complete blocks. They sound formal, solemn or slightly ironic, so use them carefully in speeches and essays.

en.g.estilo.descripcion_l: Choosing grammatical structures to control tone, emphasis and formality.

en.l.presentarse.oficial: Greetings; Giving personal information; Personal information
en.l.presentarse.descripcion_l: Greeting people and introducing yourself: personal details and jobs.
en.l.presentarse.descripcion_larga_l: These are the first words of every conversation: greetings (Hello, Good morning), goodbyes (Bye, See you later, Good night) and basic personal information (My name is…, I'm from…, I work as…). Choose the greeting for the time of day and the situation. Remember: we say I'm 30 (not I have 30), I'm a doctor (with a) and Good night only when we leave or go to bed.

en.l.numeros-tiempo.descripcion_l: Counting, prices, telling the time, and days and months.
en.l.numeros-tiempo.descripcion_larga_l: This unit covers the basics of numbers and time in English: cardinal and ordinal numbers, prices, telling the time, days of the week, months and dates. You will also practise the prepositions at, on and in: at nine o'clock, on Monday, in June. Remember that days and months start with a capital letter and that we say dates with ordinal numbers.

en.l.familia.descripcion_l: Family members, relationships and describing people.
en.l.familia.descripcion_larga_l: This sheet has the basic words to talk about your family: parents, brothers and sisters, aunts, uncles, cousins and in-laws. It also has words to describe people: tall, short, friendly, shy, funny. Be careful: parents means your father and mother, siblings means brothers and sisters, and sympathetic does not mean «simpático». Use friendly or nice instead.

en.l.vida-diaria.titulo_l: Describing habits and routines / Leisure activities
en.l.vida-diaria.oficial: Describing habits and routines; Leisure activities
en.l.vida-diaria.descripcion_l: Everyday actions, the home and free time.
en.l.vida-diaria.descripcion_larga_l: This unit gives you the words to talk about a normal day: get up, have a shower, have breakfast, go to work, get home and go to bed. It also covers housework, like do the shopping and make the bed, and free time. Use the present simple and frequency adverbs: I usually get up at seven. I'm always tired on Mondays.

en.l.comida.titulo_l: Food and drink / Things in the town, shops and shopping
en.l.comida.oficial: Food and drink; Things in the town, shops and shopping
en.l.comida.descripcion_l: Food, eating out at a restaurant, quantities and basic shopping.
en.l.comida.descripcion_larga_l: Basic words for food, containers and quantities, and the phrases you need to order in a café or restaurant. You will use them from your first day in an English-speaking country. Many food words are uncountable (bread, milk, rice), so we say some bread or a loaf of bread, not a bread. Polite phrases like I'd like are also important.

en.l.ciudad.titulo_l: Things in the town, shops and shopping / Directions
en.l.ciudad.oficial: Things in the town, shops and shopping; Directions
en.l.ciudad.descripcion_l: Places in town, transport, and asking for and giving directions.
en.l.ciudad.descripcion_larga_l: This vocabulary helps you move around a town. You learn the names of places, like the bank, the chemist's, the town hall or the library, and how to ask for directions: Excuse me, how do I get to the station? To give directions, use simple instructions: go straight on, turn left, take the second street on the right. Remember: a library lends books, a bookshop sells them.

en.l.trabajo-estudios.descripcion_l: Jobs, work tasks and education or training.
en.l.trabajo-estudios.descripcion_larga_l: This unit gives you the words you need to talk about your job, your daily tasks and your studies: job and work, colleague, manager, degree, subject, pass or fail an exam. You use them when you introduce yourself, in a job interview or in an oral exam. Be careful with false friends: a career is your working life, not your university degree.

en.l.viajes.descripcion_l: Bookings, airports, hotels and dealing with problems while travelling.
en.l.viajes.descripcion_larga_l: This unit covers the words you need when you travel: booking a room or a ticket, finding your gate or platform, checking in and out of a hotel and solving problems such as a delayed flight or lost luggage. Learn the difference between travel, trip and journey, and between miss (a train) and lose (an object). Remember that luggage is uncountable.

en.l.salud.descripcion_l: Symptoms, visiting the doctor and healthy habits.
en.l.salud.descripcion_larga_l: This vocabulary helps you say what is wrong with you, describe your symptoms and talk to a doctor or a chemist. Learn the words for parts of the body, the -ache words (headache, toothache) and useful phrases like make an appointment or get better. Be careful: constipated does not mean that you have a cold, and a recipe is for cooking, not for medicine.

en.l.dinero.descripcion_l: Paying, banking, and buying and returning things.
en.l.dinero.descripcion_larga_l: This unit teaches the words and phrases you need to pay for things, talk about prices, use a bank and take things back to a shop. Many money verbs have fixed prepositions: you pay for something and spend money on something. Be careful with borrow and lend: you borrow from someone, but you lend something to someone.

en.l.clima.descripcion_l: Describing the weather and the seasons.
en.l.clima.descripcion_larga_l: Words to talk about the weather, the seasons, weather forecasts and the climate of a place. The weather is one of the most common topics of conversation in English, especially in Britain, and it appears in many speaking exams. Spanish speakers often say «it makes cold» instead of «it's cold», and they mix up weather (today) and climate (usual conditions).

en.l.gustos.descripcion_l: Saying what you like and prefer, and giving simple opinions (I think that…).
en.l.gustos.descripcion_larga_l: This card covers words and phrases to talk about what you like and dislike (like, love, enjoy, hate, can't stand), to say what you prefer (prefer, would rather) and to give a simple opinion (What do you think of it?). Remember that each verb has its own pattern: enjoy + -ing, would like + to, prefer A to B.

en.l.medios.titulo_l: Media / News, lifestyles and current affairs
en.l.medios.oficial: Media; News, lifestyles and current affairs
en.l.medios.descripcion_l: The press, radio and social media, and talking about the news.
en.l.medios.descripcion_larga_l: This unit gives you the words to talk about how you get information: newspapers, television, radio and social media. You will learn words like headline, coverage, broadcast and biased. Remember that news is uncountable and takes a singular verb, that an editorial is not a publishing company, and that we say on TV and on social media but in the newspaper.

en.l.medio-ambiente.descripcion_larga_l: This unit gives you the basic words to talk about environmental problems, their causes and possible solutions: pollution, climate change, renewable energy, waste and recycling. The environment is a very common topic in debates, essays and speaking exams. Remember that many of these nouns are uncountable, and learn useful phrasal verbs such as cut down on, run out of and throw away.

en.l.conectores-1.titulo_l: Connecting words expressing cause and effect, contrast etc
en.l.conectores-1.oficial: Connecting words expressing cause and effect, contrast etc; Linkers: sequential – past time
en.l.conectores-1.descripcion_l: Basic linkers for cause, consequence, contrast, addition and sequence.
en.l.conectores-1.descripcion_larga_l: Linking words connect ideas and make a text or a talk easy to follow. We use them to add information (moreover), to contrast (although, despite), to give reasons and results (because of, so, as a result), to order ideas (firstly, finally) and to conclude (to sum up). Be careful with what comes after each one: a full sentence or just a noun.

en.l.opinar.titulo_l: Expressing opinions / Expressing agreement and disagreement
en.l.opinar.oficial: Expressing opinions; Expressing agreement and disagreement
en.l.opinar.descripcion_l: Useful phrases for giving opinions, agreeing, disagreeing and challenging other views.
en.l.opinar.descripcion_larga_l: This unit gives you useful expressions to give your opinion, ask for other people's opinions, agree completely or partly, and disagree politely. You will learn phrases like in my opinion, as far as I'm concerned, I couldn't agree more and I'm afraid I disagree. Remember that agree is a verb, so we say I agree, not I am agree.

en.l.narrar.oficial: Describing past experiences & storytelling; Linkers: sequential – past time
en.l.narrar.descripcion_l: Time and sequence markers for telling stories and describing experiences.
en.l.narrar.descripcion_larga_l: This unit gives you the words you need to tell a story or talk about an experience: how to start (one day, a few years ago), how to put events in order (first, then, afterwards), how to show that things happened at the same time (while, meanwhile) or suddenly, and how to finish (eventually, in the end, at last). These words help your listener follow the story easily.

en.l.phrasal-tematicos.descripcion_l: Phrasal verbs grouped by topic: work, relationships, money and problems.
en.l.phrasal-tematicos.descripcion_larga_l: This card groups common phrasal verbs by topic: work (take on, lay off, set up, hand in), relationships (get on with, fall out, make up, break up, bring up) and money and problems (pay back, save up, cut back on, sort out, call off, put off). Learning them in groups helps you remember them and use them naturally when you speak.

en.l.sociedad.descripcion_larga_l: This vocabulary helps you talk about social issues and public policy: equality, immigration, an ageing population, housing, unemployment, education and the welfare state. Many of these nouns are uncountable, like housing and poverty. Groups of people are often named with the + adjective, such as the elderly or the homeless, and they take a plural verb. Remember that a British public school is actually a private school.

en.l.economia.descripcion_l: Growth, employment, inflation, markets and trade.
en.l.economia.descripcion_larga_l: This unit covers the economic vocabulary you meet in newspapers and reports: growth, inflation, interest rates, unemployment, company results and international trade. It is essential for summarising economic news and presenting economic topics in English. Watch out for false friends: economics is the science, the economy is a country's economic system, and a company's benefit is called profit.

en.l.politica.descripcion_l: Government, parliament, elections and the European Union.
en.l.politica.descripcion_larga_l: This vocabulary helps you talk about governments, parliaments, elections and the institutions of the European Union. You will learn how a bill becomes an act, how voters choose their representatives and how coalitions are formed. Be careful with policy and politics: a policy is a specific plan or measure, while politics is the general activity of governing and competing for power.

en.l.ciencia-tecnologia.descripcion_l: Research, the digital world and artificial intelligence.
en.l.ciencia-tecnologia.descripcion_larga_l: This vocabulary helps you talk about scientific research, innovation, the internet and artificial intelligence. Many words look international, but the word partners are different: we carry out or conduct research, we do not make it. Research and evidence are uncountable, so we never say a research or evidences. To actualize does not mean to update. Learn words like breakthrough, findings, device and data breach in context.

en.l.conectores-2.oficial: Linking devices, logical markers; Conceding a point
en.l.conectores-2.descripcion_l: Linkers for building an argument: concession, reformulation, giving examples and concluding.
en.l.conectores-2.descripcion_larga_l: These linking words help you build a clear argument: to concede a point (admittedly, even so), to contrast ideas (whereas, on the contrary), to rephrase (in other words, that is), to give examples (for instance, such as), to add (moreover) and to conclude (to sum up, all in all). They are essential in essays, reports, summaries and formal presentations.

en.l.matizar.oficial: Expressing opinions tentatively, hedging; Expressing certainty, probability, doubt
en.l.matizar.descripcion_l: Expressing probability, caution and degrees of certainty.
en.l.matizar.descripcion_larga_l: Hedging means expressing an idea carefully, without sounding too sure. We use modal verbs such as may and might, verbs like seem, appear and tend, adverbs like arguably and apparently, and phrases such as to some extent. In formal English, especially in reports, presentations and academic writing, hedging makes you sound balanced, honest and professional instead of arrogant or careless.

en.l.tendencias-cifras.descripcion_l: Saying that figures rise, fall or level off; percentages and comparisons.
en.l.tendencias-cifras.descripcion_larga_l: This vocabulary helps you describe charts, statistics and economic data. You need verbs such as rise, fall, soar, plummet or level off, adjectives and adverbs such as sharp, slight, dramatically or slightly, and the right prepositions: rise by 2% (the change) and rise to 5% (the final level). Remember that rise has no object, while raise needs one, and that the gap between two percentages is measured in percentage points.

en.l.colocaciones.descripcion_l: Natural word combinations, such as make a decision.
en.l.colocaciones.descripcion_larga_l: Collocations are words that native speakers naturally use together, like make a decision, heavy traffic or pay attention. There is often no logical rule, so you need to learn them as fixed chunks. Good collocations make your English sound natural instead of translated. Spanish speakers often choose the wrong verb (do a mistake) or the wrong adjective (strong rain).

en.l.falsos-amigos.descripcion_l: English words that look like Spanish words but mean something different.
en.l.falsos-amigos.descripcion_larga_l: False friends are English words that look like Spanish words but mean something different. Actually means «en realidad», not «actualmente»; sensible means «sensato»; a library is a place where you borrow books, not where you buy them. Because they look familiar, Spanish speakers use them without thinking. Learn each false friend together with the correct English word for the Spanish meaning.

en.l.registro.oficial: Formal and informal registers; Colloquial language
en.l.registro.descripcion_l: Choosing formal, neutral or colloquial words to suit the situation.
en.l.registro.descripcion_larga_l: English often has two or three ways to say the same thing. Formal words usually come from Latin (obtain, require, purchase); neutral or informal words are often short words or phrasal verbs (get, need, buy, put off). In formal writing we avoid contractions and slang like wanna. In conversation, very formal words sound stiff: I'll help you is more natural than I will assist you.

en.l.formacion-palabras.descripcion_larga_l: Word formation shows how one root can give a whole family of words: employ, employment, employer, employee, unemployed. Suffixes such as -ment, -ity, -able or -ly change the type of word, and prefixes such as un-, im-, mis- or re- change its meaning. First decide what kind of word the sentence needs, then choose the right ending or beginning.

en.l.prensa-idiomatica.descripcion_l: Idiomatic phrases frequently used in newspaper articles and editorials.
en.l.prensa-idiomatica.descripcion_larga_l: Newspapers in English use many fixed idioms, often taken from sport, war, sailing or the weather: a level playing field, to weather the storm, to bite the bullet. Many have a Spanish equivalent, but the image is sometimes different. These expressions are fixed, so you cannot change their words. Learn to recognise them when you read, and use one or two carefully when you speak.

en.l.abstracto.descripcion_l: Nouns for ideas, processes and qualities.
en.l.abstracto.descripcion_larga_l: Abstract nouns such as rationale, trade-off, accountability or hindsight let you talk about ideas in a precise, formal way. They are very common in reports, economic news and essays. Learn each noun with its preposition (reliance on, insight into, commitment to) and watch out for false friends: consistent means coherent, and awareness, not conscience, is what a campaign raises.

en.l.exposicion.titulo_l: Discourse markers to structure formal speech
en.l.exposicion.oficial: Discourse markers to structure formal speech; Markers to structure and signpost formal and informal speech and writing
en.l.exposicion.descripcion_l: Phrases for opening a talk, linking its parts, gaining time and closing.
en.l.exposicion.descripcion_larga_l: Signposting language guides your listeners through a talk. It tells them what you will talk about, how the talk is organised, when you move to a new point, and when you are finishing. Useful phrases include I've divided my presentation into three parts, Let's now turn to, A case in point is, and To recap. Prepare two or three phrases for each function before an oral exam.

en.l.sintesis.descripcion_l: Reporting verbs and paraphrasing for summarising and rewording ideas.
en.l.sintesis.descripcion_larga_l: Reporting verbs such as argue, claim, acknowledge, warn or call for help you summarise what an author says and show his or her attitude. Choosing the right verb is part of a good summary: claim suggests doubt, acknowledge means the author admits a point against his own view. Paraphrasing techniques, such as changing a verb into a noun or using the passive, help you avoid copying the original text.

en.l.debate.descripcion_l: Asking for clarification, qualifying your position and drawing conclusions in a debate or Q&A.
en.l.debate.descripcion_larga_l: This unit gives you useful phrases for debates and for answering questions from an examining board. You will learn how to ask for clarification, agree or disagree politely, accept part of an argument before you object, interrupt, and close your answer. In English, direct disagreement can sound rude, so speakers usually soften it with phrases like «I see your point, but…».

en.l.derecho-justicia.descripcion_larga_l: This unit covers the legal vocabulary you find in newspapers and official documents: types of laws, courts and legal professionals, the stages of criminal and civil cases, and fundamental rights. Because the common law system is different from the Spanish one, many terms do not match exactly. Pay special attention to false friends like sentence, process and jurisprudence.

en.l.cultura.descripcion_larga_l: This unit gives you the language to discuss books, films, plays, exhibitions and cultural heritage at an advanced level. Beyond basic nouns, it focuses on the collocations critics use: a story is set somewhere, a film stars an actor, a play is staged, and a museum features works. It also helps you avoid false friends such as argument (not plot) and critic (not review).

en.l.estilo.descripcion_l: Near-synonyms with different shades of meaning, irony and understatement.
en.l.estilo.descripcion_larga_l: At the highest level, choosing a word means choosing an attitude. Many near-synonyms describe the same thing but praise or criticise it: thrifty or stingy, determined or stubborn. This sheet also practises euphemisms, such as to let someone go, and British understatement, such as not exactly or hardly the most. These forms help you sound polite and understand what people really mean.

en.l.alusiones.descripcion_l: Proverbs and cultural allusions that native speakers take for granted.
en.l.alusiones.descripcion_larga_l: Proverbs and cultural allusions to the Bible, Greek myths, history, Shakespeare or modern novels appear in newspapers and speeches without any explanation. Writers often quote only half a proverb (When in Rome…) and expect readers to complete it. Learning the English versions, instead of translating Spanish proverbs word for word, helps you understand irony and tone and sound natural at an advanced level.

en.l.especializado.descripcion_l: Specialist terms from finance, diplomacy and international trade.
en.l.especializado.descripcion_larga_l: This sheet covers the specialised English used in finance, monetary policy, international trade, the WTO and economic diplomacy: spread, basis point, default, hedge, quota, rules of origin, dispute settlement. Each term should be learnt with its usual partner words, for example to default on a debt or to impose sanctions on a country. Precise terms matter: one wrong word can change the meaning of a report.
